definition: Bolster means to strengthen or support something, propping it up so that it does not sag or fail.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word bolster. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know bolster should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Stagehands slid extra supports beneath the outdoor stage to bolster it before the festival crowd arrived.
Support is weaker than bolster: you can support a proposal just by voting for it, while bolstering it means actively shoring it up with evidence or resources when it starts to wobble.
Fortify is stronger than bolster: a coach bolsters a nervous team with steady encouragement, while a general fortifies a position until it can withstand a direct assault.

Reinforce means to strengthen something by adding more of what it is already made of — more steel in a wall, more troops on a line. Bolster props up whatever is sagging, and the support can be a different kind of thing entirely: fresh data for a claim, kind words for morale. Reinforce thickens; bolster shores up.

Prop up is the everyday, hands-on phrase: you prop up a shelf with a brick, visibly and often temporarily. Bolster does the same job in more formal dress and moves easily into the abstract, where arguments, currencies, and confidence all get bolstered. Prop up sounds like a stopgap; bolster sounds like real backing.

Boost means to push something higher than it was — boost sales, boost a signal. A boost lifts the level; a bolster steadies it. You boost what you want to raise; you bolster what you cannot afford to let collapse.
to drain the strength from something
to wear away strength or energy little by little

The original noun is still alive: furniture shops sell bolsters, the long cylinder pillows that hold a reader upright in bed. The verb kept the pillow's old job, and English quietly moved it from sofas to arguments, economies, and morale.
Bolster means to strengthen or support something, propping it up so that it does not sag or fail.
When the peso slid for the third week in a row, the central bank began spending its reserves to bolster the currency before panic could set in.
The currency was losing strength fast, and the bank threw its own resources behind it to hold it up.
Adding support to something that is weakening — with money, evidence, or encouragement — is exactly what bolster means.
Neutral; leans formal in news and academic writing
Bolster almost always takes an abstract object: you bolster confidence, an argument, or a sagging economy.
Watch the spelling trap with holster, one letter away but a case for carrying a pistol — and if a furniture label says bolster, that is the noun, the long firm pillow the verb grew from.
